# The wall and the standard error {.unnumbered} *Roughly 45 minutes, and the reason the session exists. Part A confirms your pre-reading with your own hands. Part C must be done before Part D: read ahead and you throw away the most useful thing you produce today.* ## Part A: warm-up, confirm the pre-reading You read that a probability is a long-run frequency, and that the proportion of heads settles towards 0.5 as flips accumulate. Confirm it, with your own seed. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Watch a probability settle :::: ::::{.task-container} Set your seed, then run one thousand flips and plot the running proportion. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} student_id <- 12345678 # <- yours session_code <- 4271 # <- from the board set_my_seed(student_id, session_code) my_run <- running_proportion(1000, prob = 0.5) ggplot(my_run, aes(flip, proportion)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") + geom_line() + scale_x_log10() + labs(x = "Number of flips (log scale)", y = "Proportion of heads") ``` ::: Where is the proportion wildest? Where does it calm down? Roughly how many flips before it stops surprising you? :::: :::
The line lurches in the first few dozen flips, sometimes wildly, then tightens onto 0.5 as the flips pile up. It will not land exactly on 0.5, and it never would in finite time. The lesson is not that the proportion reaches the truth, it is that it stops wandering away from it. That "stops wandering" is the frequentist definition of probability, and it is the same behaviour you are about to see in a quantity that matters far more than a coin: a sample mean.
## Part B: one sample of beans There is a jar of beans. What is the mean mass of a bean in it? You cannot weigh them all, so you weigh ten. That is the whole problem of statistics in one sentence: you want a fact about a population, and you can afford only a sample. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} my_sample <- population |> slice_sample(n = 10) my_sample ``` ::: The book runs on the demonstration seed, so these ten beans are not yours. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} demo_sample ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| bean_id| mass_g| |-------:|------:| | 1825| 0.659| | 191| 0.506| | 1466| 0.670| | 1261| 0.486| | 1278| 0.570| | 1042| 0.542| | 115| 0.503| | 655| 0.540| | 1088| 0.488| | 797| 0.519|
::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(demo_sample$mass_g) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.5483 ``` ::: ::: Ask your neighbour what they got. It is different. Hold onto that; it is Part C, and it is the only interesting thing that happens today. ### The standard deviation, by hand, once The SD asks: how far is a typical bean from the mean bean? You cannot average the raw deviations, because they cancel to zero by construction. So square them, average, and square-root back into grams. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} demo_sample |> mutate( deviation = mass_g - mean(mass_g), squared_deviation = deviation^2 ) |> summarise( n = n(), mean_g = mean(mass_g), variance = sum(squared_deviation) / (n - 1), sd_g = sqrt(variance) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| n| mean_g| variance| sd_g| |--:|------:|---------:|---------:| | 10| 0.5483| 0.0044291| 0.0665517|
::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sd(demo_sample$mass_g) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.06655165 ``` ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Your own SD, and a question :::: ::::{.task-container} Run the longhand pipeline on **your** sample and confirm it matches `sd()`. Then, without running anything: if you replaced `squared_deviation` with the raw `deviation` and averaged that instead, what number would you get, and why? :::: :::
You would get **zero**, exactly, for any dataset ever collected. The mean is by definition the point from which deviations sum to zero, so a spread measure built on unsquared deviations is guaranteed to return nothing useful. Squaring is one fix; taking absolute values is another, and gives the mean absolute deviation, a perfectly sensible statistic that history did not happen to crown.
:::{.callout-note} ## Why `n - 1` and not `n`? You measured deviations from *your* sample mean, not the true mean, and the sample mean sits in the middle of your own data by construction, so those deviations run slightly small. Dividing by `n - 1` compensates. Worth thirty seconds, no more, in week one. ::: ## Part C: your prediction Before the wall goes up, commit. Look at Box 2 of your prediction sheet if you have it; if not, answer here. **The spread of everyone's sample means, compared with the spread of individual beans, will be:** **Going from n = 10 to n = 40 changes the spread of the sample means by a factor of roughly:** **Do not change these once the reveal is on screen.** A prediction quietly revised is worth nothing, to you or to your marks. ## Part D: the wall On the wall, each of you posted one sticky note: one sample mean, from one sample of ten. The computer does it ten thousand times while you read this. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} many_means <- tibble(replicate = 1:10000) |> mutate(sample_mean = map_dbl(replicate, \(i) draw_one_mean(n = 10))) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} comparison <- bind_rows( population |> transmute(value = mass_g, what = "Individual beans"), many_means |> transmute(value = sample_mean, what = "Means of samples of 10") ) ggplot(comparison, aes(x = value, colour = what, linetype = what)) + geom_density(linewidth = 0.9) + colorspace::scale_colour_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 3") + labs(x = "Mass (g)", y = "Density", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "top") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Individual beans against means of samples of ten, on the same axis, from the same jar. The means cluster far more tightly.](02-wall-and-se_files/figure-html/fig-wall-1.png){#fig-wall fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: Same jar, same axis, and the means are far tighter. It stops being surprising the moment you say it aloud: to get an extreme mean you need ten extreme beans at once, and that is much harder than drawing one. ### The standard error The spread of that second curve has a name. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} se_empirical <- sd(many_means$sample_mean) se_empirical ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.0262943 ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-important} ## The sentence **The standard deviation describes data. The standard error describes an estimate.** `sd(my_sample$mass_g)` answers: how far is a typical bean from the mean bean? `sd(many_means$sample_mean)` answers: how far is a typical sample mean from the true mean? Different numbers, different things. The first is about beans. The second is about you, and how wrong you probably are. ::: **Which of these shrinks as you collect more data?** ### The formula is a shortcut for the wall You met $SE = SD/\sqrt{n}$ in the pre-reading as a formula. It is not a separate fact; it predicts what the wall would look like without building it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble( method = c("Empirical: SD of 10,000 simulated means", "Formula: sample SD / sqrt(10)", "Truth: population SD / sqrt(10)"), value = c(se_empirical, sd(demo_sample$mass_g) / sqrt(10), sigma / sqrt(10)) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|method | value| |:---------------------------------------|---------:| |Empirical: SD of 10,000 simulated means | 0.0262943| |Formula: sample SD / sqrt(10) | 0.0210455| |Truth: population SD / sqrt(10) | 0.0262388|
::: ::: All three agree, to within noise. That agreement is why we trust the computer for the rest of the module: it reproduces something you built by hand, out of beans, in a room. ## Part E: what n does ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} means_by_n <- expand_grid(n = c(5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160), replicate = 1:2000) |> mutate(sample_mean = map_dbl(n, \(k) draw_one_mean(n = k))) se_by_n <- means_by_n |> summarise(se_observed = sd(sample_mean), .by = n) |> mutate(se_predicted = sigma / sqrt(n)) ggplot(se_by_n, aes(x = n, y = se_observed)) + geom_line(aes(y = se_predicted), linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "dashed") + geom_point(size = 3, colour = colorspace::qualitative_hcl(1, palette = "Dark 3")) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = se_by_n$n, transform = "log2") + labs(x = "Sample size, n (log2 scale)", y = "Standard error of the mean (g)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Standard error against sample size. Points are simulated; the dashed line is sigma/sqrt(n). Quadrupling n halves the standard error.](02-wall-and-se_files/figure-html/fig-by-n-1.png){#fig-by-n fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: :::{.callout-warning} ## The bit that costs money The standard error falls with $\sqrt{n}$, not with $n$. To halve your uncertainty you must **quadruple** your sample. To halve it again, quadruple it again. Sixteen times the fieldwork for a fourfold improvement. This is the most expensive fact in experimental biology, and it is why sample size is settled before data collection, not after. ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Reconcile (graded) :::: ::::{.task-container} This is Box 5 of your sheet. 1. Re-run this chapter with **your** seed and `n = 40`. Check your empirical SE against `sigma / sqrt(40)`. 2. Write three lines: what you predicted, what you got, and what the class wall gave. 3. Write one more: why they agree, or why they differ. A wrong prediction honestly reconciled beats a right one with no reasoning attached. :::: :::
**`sd(many_means$sample_mean) * sqrt(10)`** returns the population SD, about 0.083 g. You have run the shortcut backwards: the wall contained the SD all along. **Setting `n = 1`** makes the two curves in @fig-wall land on top of each other. A "sample mean" of one bean is just a bean, so the sampling distribution of the mean *is* the distribution of the beans, and $\sigma/\sqrt{1} = \sigma$. The SD is simply the SE of a sample of one; they were never different kinds of thing.
:::{.callout-note} ## The recurring question The wall has one sticky note per **student**, not per bean. If two of you had shared a sample and posted two notes from the same ten beans, would the wall still be honest? Hold the question. It has a name, and a body count, in session 8. :::
